title: Bar Stock Take
summary: How bar stock is counted daily and monthly, how variances are investigated, and why a second person must verify every count.
body:
## 1. PURPOSE

To count and track bar stock accurately for financial accountability, consistent operations, quality control and reliable reporting.

## 2. SCOPE

This SOP applies to all bar staff and Duty Managers and covers the restaurant bar, the bar store and the back store.

## 3. ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES

### 3.1 Bartenders

- Keep the bar clean and hygienic.
- Complete the opening and closing checklists.
- Complete the daily prep sheet counts.
- Keep the waste log up to date (breakages, spillages and spoiled stock).
- Rotate stock using FIFO (first in, first out).

### 3.2 Duty Manager

- Inspect the bar areas.
- Make sure checklists and procedures are followed.
- Sign off the daily checklists and counts.
- Investigate and document variances.
- Address performance or hygiene issues.

## 4. BAR STOCK TAKE

### 4.1 Schedule and preparation

| **Count**       | **Areas**                     | **When**                              |
|-----------------|-------------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| **Daily count** | Bar and bar store             | At the end of the night shift         |
| **Full count**  | Back store, bar and bar store | Monthly, on the last day of the month |

- **Organisation:** keep all storage areas neat and organised so counts are quick and accurate.
- **Stock issues:** stock may only be issued under a manager’s supervision, and every issue must be recorded in Pilot.

### 4.2 How to count

Bar stock is counted in two groups:

### A. Full units (sealed)

- Count all full cases and unopened bottles in the bar store and the under-bar fridges.
- Count systematically, from left to right and from top to bottom.

### B. Part units (opened stock)

- **Spirits and liqueurs:** use the measuring tool provided (the tot ruler or stock measure) to read the volume left.
- **Kegs:** weigh the keg, then subtract the known weight of an empty keg. The difference is the beer left in the keg (1 kg of beer is about 1 litre). Use the same method every day.

### 4.3 Reconciliation and variances

When the physical count is complete, the Duty Manager compares it with the Pilot prep sheet. If there is a difference (a variance), the Duty Manager must investigate, find the cause and record the findings.

### Common causes of variances

- Spillages or breakages that were not recorded.
- Over-pouring by bar staff.
- Complimentary drinks that were not recorded.
- Stock loss or theft.

### 4.4 After the count

- **Check against the waste log:** reconcile every variance against the daily waste log. Missing stock that is not recorded as a breakage or spillage points to a control failure and must be investigated immediately.
- **Ordering:** use the final counts to prepare the order for the following week.

## 5. CONTROL MEASURE: SEGREGATION OF DUTIES

The person who places liquor orders may not be the only person who does the physical count. A second person must always verify the count, so that stock records cannot be manipulated.

## 6. RELATED DOCUMENTS

- PEL-MAN-001 Pilot POS Operating Manual (section 6, Daily bar stock take)
- PEL-SOP-006 Changing Beer Kegs and Line Sanitation
- PEL-SOP-004 Duty Manager Procedure
